title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: WHAT A LATIN TELEPHONE CALL SOUNDS LIKE IS A DECISION, NOT A DISCOVERY. No Roman made one, so the words come from one named source — the Vatican's lexicon of recent Latin and the settled usage of people who speak Latin today — and nothing is coined in this module. tēlephōnum for the instrument, nūntius for a message. The same honesty en-ar needed for Modern Standard Arabic and en-sa for spoken Sanskrit: you are being taught a living agreement, not an ancient fact.

THE CALL OPENS AND CLOSES WITH L1-M2's WORDS, UNCHANGED: salvē to open, valē to close. There is no Latin 'hello?' for a telephone, so the greeting that works in the street works here, and the caller names themselves with L1-M7's hīc — Mārcus hīc est, 'Marcus here'. That means the whole module adds no social vocabulary at all, only nouns and verbs.

quis IS THE SIXTH qu- WORD AND HERE IS THE WHOLE FAMILY: ubi where, quō to where, unde from where, quid what, quod because, quis who. Six short words, one family, parted by their vowels. quis takes the he/she shape of the verb, because an unknown person is a third person — and Quis est? against Quid est? is one letter between asking who someone is and what is wrong.

THE MODULE HAS BOTH OF L1-M6's FUTURES SIDE BY SIDE, and which verb takes which is not guessable from the meaning: relinquam and accipiam take -am, tēlephōnābō and tēlephōnābit take -bō and -bit. The coined verb is the regular one, because whoever built it built it on the easy conjugation — a modern word is a tidy word, and the ancient ones are where the irregularity lives.

THE VOCATIVE IS STILL DEFERRED, AND THIS IS THE MODULE THAT WANTS IT MOST. Speaking someone's name into a telephone is exactly where Mārce belongs. L1 got away without it because every name it greeted — Iūlia, magister, discipula — has an address shape identical to its subject shape, and Mārcus does not. So this module writes Mārcus as a subject only, names the gap, and leaves Mārce to a later level.

words.note: 'Hello' — literally 'be well'. L1-M2's greeting, and it serves for every hour and every situation, a telephone call included, because Latin has no separate word for answering one.
A Roman man's name, and the subject shape. Addressing him would need a different shape, which this course has not taught — here he is naming himself, so the subject shape is right.
'Here'. L1-M7's word, and Mārcus hīc est is how a caller names themselves: 'Marcus here', exactly as in English.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: There is no Latin 'hello?' for a telephone, so the call opens with the greeting L1-M2 taught for walking up to someone in the street. The module is not hiding a word from you: no Roman ever answered a phone, and this is the living-Latin community's answer.

variations.changed: L1-M2's plural greeting, for more than one listener
the greeting dropped, which is abrupt but not wrong

sentences.usage: Said the moment a call connects.

words.note: 'Who', asking. The sixth qu- word: ubi where, quō to where, unde from where, quid what, quod because, quis who. Six words, one family, and only the vowels part them.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: Two words, and they are one bar and one letter from a sentence you already know. Quid est? is 'what is it?' and Quis est? is 'who is it?' — and on a telephone the difference decides whether you are asking about a person or a problem.

mistake.why: the what-question asked about a person. Both are correct Latin sentences and they differ by one letter, so nothing warns you — you simply find out you asked what someone was rather than who.

sentences.usage: Said when a call comes in.

sentences.cue: I do not have a telephone.

words.note: 'Telephone' — a modern word, from the Vatican's lexicon of recent Latin and the usage of people who speak Latin now. It is neuter, so it does not change between subject and object.
'Not', in front of what it denies. L1-M3's word.
'I have': habeō 'I have', habēs 'you have', habet 'he has'. L1-M1's verb.

sentences.trap: tēlephōnum is neuter, so it looks the same whether you have one or one is sitting there. After nine modules of endings moving, the neuter nouns — vīnum, nōmen, auxilium, this — are the ones that stay still, and there are enough of them to be worth noticing.

variations.changed: the same shape as a subject, which proves it does not move

variations.cue: You do not have a telephone.

sentences.usage: Said when someone asks how to reach you.

words.note: 'Message' — nūntius as the subject, nūntium as the thing left or taken. It also means a messenger, which is what it meant first.
'I leave behind' — relinquō 'I leave', relinquit 'he leaves', relinquam 'I shall leave'. English 'relinquish' is the same word, and the future follows L1-M6's -am.

sentences.trap: The future of this verb is relinquam, not relinquābō. L1-M6 taught two futures — labōrābō from a first-conjugation verb and legam from a third — and relinquō belongs to the second family, so it takes the -am. The verb tells you which; the ending of the 'I' form is the clue.

variations.changed: the other half of the job

variations.cue: I am not leaving a message.

sentences.usage: Said to whoever answers instead of the person you wanted.

words.note: 'Message' — nūntius as the subject, nūntium as the thing left or taken. It also means a messenger, which is what it meant first.
'I receive, I take' — accipiō 'I take', accipit 'he takes', accipiam 'I shall take'. English 'accept' is the same word, and its future is the -am kind.

sentences.trap: Two verbs, one noun, and the whole job of answering someone else's telephone. accipiō is 'take' in the sense of receiving — it is not the verb for picking something up — and that is the reading English 'accept' preserves.

variations.cue: I take a message and leave one.

sentences.usage: Said when the person wanted is not there.

words.note: 'Who', asking. The sixth qu- word: ubi where, quō to where, unde from where, quid what, quod because, quis who. Six words, one family, and only the vowels part them.
'Message' — nūntius as the subject, nūntium as the thing left or taken. It also means a messenger, which is what it meant first.
'He leaves' — relinquō's third-person shape. The question word is the subject, so the verb is the he/she shape even though nobody has been named.

sentences.trap: quis takes the he/she shape of the verb. It is asking about one unknown person, and Latin treats an unknown person as a third person — so the verb has already decided something the question has not.

variations.changed: the shortest form of the question

sentences.usage: Said when you missed who spoke.

words.note: 'Again'. It never changes shape and it comes before the verb, like L1-M4's saepe and semper.
'I shall telephone' — a modern verb on the modern noun: tēlephōnō 'I telephone', tēlephōnat 'he telephones', tēlephōnābō 'I shall'. It takes L1-M6's -bō, because it was built to be regular.

sentences.trap: This verb is the OTHER future. relinquam and accipiam take -am; tēlephōnābō takes -bō, because whoever coined it built it on the first conjugation, which is the easy one. A word made up in the twentieth century was made to be regular.
sentences.sound: I-te-rum tē-le-phō-NĀ-bō. Seven syllables, and the stress lands on the long ā of the future.

variations.changed: a taught verb under the same adverb

sentences.usage: Said to end a call that got nowhere.
sentences.mnemonic: A modern verb is a regular verb.

words.note: 'Who', asking. The sixth qu- word: ubi where, quō to where, unde from where, quid what, quod because, quis who. Six words, one family, and only the vowels part them.
'He will telephone' — the -bit future, which is L1-M6's labōrābit on a modern verb. Regular all the way through, which is the point of a coined word.

sentences.trap: Two words and both of them are new kinds of thing: a question word that behaves like a name, and a verb nobody in Rome could have said. The grammar around it is entirely L1's — that is what makes a coinage usable.

words.note: 'Goodbye' — literally 'be well', and L1-M2's word. It ends a call exactly as it ends a conversation in the street, because it is the same farewell.
'Again', unchanging and before the verb.
'I shall telephone' — the modern verb with L1-M6's -bō future.

sentences.trap: The call closes the way it opened: with L1-M2's word, unmodified. salvē and valē carried every greeting and farewell in the course and they carry this one too, which means the whole telephone module adds no social vocabulary at all — only nouns and verbs.

sentences.display: Mārcus tēlephōnum nōn habet; nūntium relinquam.
sentences.cue: Marcus does not have a telephone; I shall leave a message.
sentences.literal: Marcus telephone not he-has message I-shall-leave

words.note: A Roman man's name in the subject shape. Talking ABOUT him needs this shape; talking TO him would need one this course has not taught.
'Telephone' — a modern word, from the Vatican's lexicon of recent Latin and the usage of people who speak Latin now. It is neuter, so it does not change between subject and object.
'He has' — habeō 'I have', habēs 'you have', habet 'he has'. L1-M1's verb.
'Message' — nūntius as the subject, nūntium as the thing left or taken. It also means a messenger, which is what it meant first.
'I shall leave' — relinquō's future, the -am kind. L1-M6 taught both futures and this verb takes the harder-looking one.

sentences.trap: Two clauses and no word joining them. Latin is content to set a fact beside its consequence with nothing but a pause, where English wants 'so' — and L1-M9's itaque is available if you want it. Naming Mārcus here is also the module's whole vocative problem: this is the subject shape, and speaking TO him would need another.

variations.display: Mārcus tēlephōnum nōn habet; itaque nūntium relinquam.
variations.cue: Marcus has no telephone, so I shall leave a message.
variations.changed: L1-M9's itaque making the consequence explicit

variations.cue: Julia has a telephone; I shall call again.
variations.changed: the other way round, with the other future

variations.display: Mārcus hīc nōn est; nūntium relinquam.
variations.cue: Marcus is not here; I shall leave a message.

mistake.why: the address shape used for someone being talked about. Mārce is how you speak TO Marcus and this course has not taught it — which is exactly why this module, where a learner most wants it, writes Mārcus and says the gap out loud.

sentences.usage: Said to yourself, working out how to reach someone.
